summary: This document specifies mechanisms for measuring packet loss and delay in TRILL networks. Performance monitoring lets operators check that they meet the service levels promised to customers and spot anomalies.

plainLanguage.summary: To know if a delivery service is good, you count lost parcels and time how long they take. This explains how to do those measurements on this type of network.

questions: what is trill oam performance monitoring
how is packet loss measured in trill
how does two-way delay measurement work
what are 1sl slm dmm and dmr messages
subtitle: How TRILL switches count lost packets and time delays between each other using small synthetic test messages.

tldr.problem: Operators of TRILL networks need to check that they deliver the service levels promised to customers and to spot anomalies, which requires measuring packet loss and delay between RBridges.
tldr.mechanism: Two RBridges exchange synthetic OAM messages that carry transmit and receive counters (for loss) or timestamps (for delay), and compare the values with simple subtraction formulas. The packet formats follow ITU-T G.8013/Y.1731.
tldr.outcome: TRILL gets one-way and two-way loss and delay measurement with defined packet formats and OpCodes. Two-way measurement is mandatory for implementations of TRILL performance monitoring; one-way is only a SHOULD.

today: RFC 7456 is a Proposed Standard from March 2015. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the TRILL fault management specification in RFC 7455.

sections.title: Why Measure Loss and Delay
sections.content:
TRILL (see RFC 6325) routes traffic between Routing Bridges (RBridges) on least-cost paths. Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) is the set of tools for detecting, isolating and reporting connection failures and performance degradation. Performance Monitoring (PM) is a key part of OAM and has two building blocks: Loss Measurement and Delay Measurement.

This RFC defines both protocols for TRILL. They are based on the PM functions of ITU-T G.8013/Y.1731. Loss Measurement sends a set of synthetic packets and compares how many were transmitted with how many were received, which gives a statistical estimate whose margin of error depends on how many packets are sent. Delay Measurement uses timestamped OAM messages to find packet delay and delay variation.

The RFC deliberately does not define loss computation by counting real user data, for the reasons given in Section 5.1 of the TRILL OAM framework.
sections.plainLanguage: A delivery company wants to know how many parcels get lost and how slow they are. So it sends test parcels and keeps score. This RFC lets network switches do the same thing.

sections.title: Maintenance Points and Measurement Styles
sections.content:
TRILL OAM runs over two kinds of Maintenance Points. A Maintenance End Point (MEP) can start and end measurements; a Maintenance Intermediate Point (MIP) sits along the path. PM lets one MEP measure any other MEP in the campus, within a specific Maintenance Domain (MD). The PM functions in this RFC do not apply to MIPs.

PM can be applied at three levels of granularity. Network-level PM runs over a dedicated test VLAN or Fine-Grained Label. Service-level PM measures actual user VLANs or labels. Flow-level PM measures a single flow by using a Flow Entropy field at the start of the OAM header, so the test packets take the same path as the monitored flow.

Paths in TRILL are not necessarily symmetric, so the two directions are measured separately when needed. In one-way PM, RB1 sends messages to RB2 and RB2 does the measuring. A MEP that implements TRILL PM SHOULD support it, and it is usually run proactively, with both sides sending periodically. In two-way PM, RB1 sends to a reflector RB2 that answers, so RB1 can see the path to RB2, the path back, and the round trip. A MEP that implements TRILL PM MUST support two-way PM, as both sender and reflector.

Because return paths can differ, the Reflector Entropy TLV from RFC 7455 lets the sender choose the Flow Entropy value used in the reply. PM can also be point-to-multipoint: the sender uses multicast and reflectors answer by unicast. To avoid reply storms, reflectors MUST wait a random delay between 0 and 2 seconds before responding, and an RBridge Scope TLV can limit who is expected to answer.
sections.plainLanguage: Two switches can play catch. Sometimes only one throws and the other keeps score. Sometimes the second one throws the ball right back, so the first can measure both ways.

sections.title: Loss Measurement
sections.content:
Loss is measured with synthetic messages and counters. In one-way measurement the sender transmits One-way Synthetic Loss (1SL) messages. It keeps a transmit counter for each peer MEP and test ID and puts the value in the Counter TX field. The receiver keeps its own receive counter, RX, and after checking that the message is addressed to it and that the MD level matches, it increments the counter. Over a measurement interval, with 'p' for the previous reading and 'c' for the current one, it computes (TXc-TXp) - (RXc-RXp).

In two-way measurement the sender transmits Synthetic Loss Messages (SLM) and the reflector answers each with a Synthetic Loss Reply (SLR) that carries the reflector's receive counter TRX. The sender then computes the far-end loss as (TXc-TXp) - (TRXc-TRXp) and the near-end loss as (TRXc-TRXp) - (RXc-RXp). Their sum is the total two-way loss. A sender may compute only the far-end loss, and then it can run flow-based PM without the Reflector Entropy TLV.

Because only counter differences are used, the counters at the two ends do not need to start from a common value. Resetting a counter during a measurement interval would give false results, so implementations SHOULD NOT clear counters during an interval. Calculations MUST include a wraparound check. Lost messages simply mean that exchange is not counted. Unicast transmission MUST be supported, multicast MAY be, and a Data TLV can be added to test different packet sizes.
sections.plainLanguage: You mail 100 numbered postcards and your friend counts how many arrive. The difference is how many got lost. The friend can also mail a postcard back with their count so you know which direction lost them.

sections.title: Delay Measurement
sections.content:
In one-way delay measurement the sender puts its transmit time T1 in a 1DM message. The receiver records the arrival time T2 and computes T2-T1. This only works if the two MEPs share a common time reference, so they MUST be time-synchronized; how is outside the scope of the RFC. If 1DM messages arrive periodically, the receiver MAY compute delay variation, and that works even without synchronization.

In two-way delay measurement the sender sends a Delay Measurement Message (DMM) with T1. The reflector records T2 on arrival and answers with a Delay Measurement Reply (DMR) carrying T1, T2 and its own transmit time T3. The sender records T4 when the DMR arrives and computes (T4-T1) - (T3-T2). This subtracts the time the reflector spent holding the packet, and it works without clock synchronization.

If the two MEPs are in fact synchronized, the sender MAY also compute the one-way delays: T2-T1 from sender to reflector and T4-T3 back. As with loss, unicast transmission MUST be supported, multicast MAY be, the reflector MUST support a Data TLV and copy it unmodified into the reply, and a DMR is always unicast.
sections.plainLanguage: You shout and start a stopwatch. Your friend notes when they heard you, waits a moment, and shouts back. You subtract their waiting time and know how long the sound really took to travel.

sections.title: Packet Formats and OpCodes
sections.content:
PM messages ride in the TRILL OAM encapsulation: a link header, the TRILL header (6 or more bytes), a 96-byte Flow Entropy field, the OAM Ethertype, the OAM Message Channel and a link trailer. The first four octets of the Message Channel are common: MD-L (maintenance domain level), Version, an 8-bit OpCode, Flags and FirstTLVOffset. The rest depends on the OpCode, and the last TLV is always an End TLV.

Loss messages (1SL, SLM, SLR) carry a Sender MEP ID, a 32-bit Test ID and a 32-bit Counter TX. The SLR adds the Reflector MEP ID and Counter TRX. Counters are 32 bits and wrap from 0xFFFFFFFF back to 0. FirstTLVOffset MUST be 16 in these messages.

Delay messages carry 64-bit timestamps that use the 64 least significant bits of the IEEE 1588-2008 timestamp format: a 32-bit seconds field followed by a 32-bit nanoseconds field. A T flag in the Flags field says proactive when set and on-demand when cleared. 1DM has T1 and room for T2; DMM and DMR have T1, T2, T3 and room for T4. FirstTLVOffset MUST be 16 in 1DM packets and 32 in DMM and DMR packets.

The OpCodes are the same as in Y.1731, taken from the range allocated by IEEE 802.1 for control by ITU-T.
sections.plainLanguage: Each test message is a form with boxes to fill in, like a sender name, a test number, a counter or a clock reading. The reply fills in the empty boxes the sender left for it.

sections.title: PM Sessions and Timing Parameters
sections.content:
Performance monitoring is made of PM sessions. A session runs between two MEPs on a specific flow and is either a Loss Measurement session or a Delay Measurement session. Loss sessions can produce metrics such as Frame Loss Ratio, availability and resiliency; delay sessions can produce Frame Delay, Inter-Frame Delay Variation, Frame Delay Range and Mean Frame Delay.

A session is defined by its PM function and by five timing terms. Start Time is when the session begins and Stop Time is when measurement ends. Message Period is the time between message transmissions. Measurement Interval is the period over which measurements are gathered and summarized; it can align with the session duration but does not have to. Repetition Time is the time between the start times of successive measurement intervals. PM messages are only sent during a session.
sections.plainLanguage: A test run has a start, a stop, how often you send a test, and how long each scorecard covers. Those settings together describe one test.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC points to the security sections of the TRILL OAM requirements, framework and fault-management documents, and to RFC 6325 for TRILL generally. It adds three PM-specific risks. An attack on a PM protocol can falsely indicate performance problems or hide real ones. Synthetic PM messages can be used to mount denial-of-service attacks on RBridges. An eavesdropper who passively watches PM messages can gather information for reconnaissance.

PM messages MAY include the OAM Authentication TLV. Because authentication needs a cryptographic algorithm, it can burden the RBridges and even distort the measurements. Operators must weigh the benefit against the possible inaccuracy, based on a system-specific threat assessment.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could fake the scorecards or flood the switches with test messages. A secret stamp on messages helps, but stamping takes time and can slow the test a little.

messages.label: SLM (Counter TX)
messages.note: Sender increments TX and puts it in the message.

messages.label: SLR (Counter TX, Counter TRX)
messages.note: Reflector increments TRX and returns it; the SLR is always unicast.

messages.label: DMM (T1)
messages.note: Sender stamps its transmission time T1.

messages.label: DMR (T1, T2, T3)
messages.note: Reflector adds its reception time T2 and transmission time T3. The sender records T4 on arrival.
